opus-5.5.text:
Fei-Fei shaped my research taste enormously, probably more than I realized while I was in the middle of my PhD.

The biggest thing I took from her is a sense of scale and ambition in choosing problems. ImageNet is the classic example. At the time, most of the field was focused on clever algorithms and small, carefully curated datasets. Fei-Fei made a bet that data itself, at a scale people thought was almost absurd, would be the thing that unlocked progress. Many people didn't believe her, and it took years of grinding work before the bet paid off. Watching that taught me that the most important research isn't always the most technically intricate. Sometimes it's identifying the bottleneck everyone else is ignoring and being stubborn enough to attack it directly.

The second thing is what I'd call a north-star mindset. She always pushed us to ask: what is the long-term goal, and does this project actually move us toward it, or is it just a nice paper? For me that north star became embodied agents, AI that doesn't just perceive the world but acts in it. A lot of my work since, from Minecraft agents to foundation models for robotics, comes from that question: how do we build general-purpose agents, and what's the ImageNet moment for action?

Third, she has a very human-centered view of AI. She'd remind us that the technology ultimately has to serve people. That has stayed with me, especially in robotics, where the end goal is machines that can help people with the physical, often tedious work in their lives.

And finally, there's a bit of the scientist's patience. ImageNet didn't become ImageNet overnight. Good taste, I think, is partly knowing what to work on and partly being willing to stay with it long enough for it to matter. That's something I try to carry into everything we do now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing ambitious problems and identifying overlooked bottlenecks, but does not say that identifying worthwhile problems is harder than figuring out how to solve them.

r002.rationale: The response describes embodied agents as the speaker’s research goal, but does not predict that future AI agents will be embodied.

fable-5.1.text:
Fei-Fei had a huge influence on me, and I think the biggest thing she taught me is to think about the "north star" first and the paper second. When I joined her lab at Stanford, I was very excited about the latest architectures, the latest tricks, and she would always pull me back and ask: what is the big problem you want to solve in ten years? Not the next conference deadline. She built ImageNet at a time when most people thought data was boring and models were the interesting part, and she was proven right. That taught me that sometimes the most important contribution is not a new algorithm, it's a new way to frame a problem, or a new benchmark, or a new environment that unlocks a whole field.

The second thing is her focus on embodiment and on agents that live in the world, not just in a dataset. Her lab was doing computer vision, but she was already thinking about robots, about agents that perceive and act. That really shaped my own trajectory toward embodied AI, toward things like Minecraft agents and eventually robotics at NVIDIA. I remember her saying that intelligence doesn't exist in a vacuum, it has to be grounded in something.

And honestly, the third thing is taste in the sense of ambition. She never discouraged a crazy idea. She would push on it, poke holes in it, but she would not say "that's too hard, do something safer." So I came out of my PhD with the sense that you should pick problems that feel a little bit scary, because if the problem doesn't scare you, probably someone else is already doing it.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes choosing a big problem and framing it well, but does not state that identifying worthwhile problems is harder than figuring out how to solve them.

r002.rationale: The response describes Fei-Fei’s influence on embodied AI and agents that perceive and act, but does not predict that future AI agents will be embodied.

astra-6.text:
I think Fei-Fei shaped my taste in how to choose a problem. It’s easy to get excited about a particular technique or a benchmark. The harder question is: if you solve this, what will we understand or be able to do that we couldn’t before?

The lesson I took from her is to start with that bigger question and then find a concrete experiment that lets you make progress. You need both the ambition and the discipline. A big vision alone isn’t enough, but you also don’t want to lose the bigger picture while optimizing the details.

That’s a mindset I try to bring to my research: be ambitious about the question, and be very honest about what your experiments actually demonstrate.

r001.rationale: It says choosing a problem is harder than getting excited about a technique or benchmark, and asks what solving it would enable us to understand or do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Fei-Fei shaped my taste in terms of asking the right questions. As a PhD student, it’s easy to get absorbed in a particular technique or benchmark. She would push you to step back: Why does this problem matter? If you solve it, what does that actually enable?

That perspective has stayed with me, especially in robotics and embodied AI. You want to build toward something bigger than an incremental improvement on a metric. And she has this combination of scientific ambition and a very human perspective—thinking about intelligence while also asking how the technology can help people. I think that’s a powerful compass for choosing what to work on.
